C. Significant Impact on Air Quality
Motor vehicle emissions are the major source of air pollution in urban areas. It has been estimated that of the pollutants in the atmosphere, 80 percent of the carbon monoxide, 65 percent of the hydrocarbons, and 60 percent of the nitrogen oxides are from motor vehicles. In 1968 estimated emissions from all transportation sources in the United States were 64 million tons (58 million MT) of carbon monoxide, 17 million tons (15.4 million MT) of hydrocarbons, and 8 million tons (7.25 million MT) of nitrogen oxides. The primary mobile source of these emissions is the gasoline powered motor vehicle. Other significant sources include aircraft, diesel-powered trucks and buses, locomotives, and marine vessels.
The normal operation of a gasoline combustion engine results in the emission and dispersion of significant amounts of contaminants into the atmosphere. The amount of air pollutants that an automobile emits depends on a number of factors - the condition of the engine, the type of fuel used, and the driving patterns during operation.
Diesel-powered motor vehicles actually emit lower quantities of most pollutants per vehicle than gasoline-powered vehicles. The generated horsepower of a diesel engine is determined and controlled by the amount of diesel fuel injected for each engine cycle. Diesel engines emit greater quantities of nitrogen oxides per vehicle than gasoline-powered engines. However, due to the fact that diesel engines have more complete combustion and less volatile fuels than spark-ignited engines, the hydrocarbon and carbon monoxide emissions are relatively lower.<sup>2</sup>
Most of the reduction in pollutants will be a result of the mobile source emission controls as specified in the 1970 amendments to the Clean Air Act. The federal government has enacted this legislation to control the amounts of emission pollutants being injected into the atmosphere by motor vehicles.
